case_study_insert.main_stem: Golden Acre Cereals (GAC) is an agricultural cooperative in the cereal milling industry, employing a workforce of 42. Founded in 2008 by Rowan Golden, the business supplies breakfast cereal to regional grocers and independent shops and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. GAC plans to invest $460,000 in a new automated flaking and packing line to cut waste, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $60,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $12.00, and produces 70,000 units a year. GAC faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and packaging waste has reached 6.1% of output.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Waste Report - Q3 2025: GAC milled 17,800 units of cereal last quarter at a defect rate of 2.9%, down from 4.2% a year ago. Packaging waste rose to 6.1% of output. Staff complaints about repetitive work increased from 19 to 31 a month. Delivery lead time averages 3.4 days. A survey of 450 shoppers found 61% preferred recyclable cartons, and 39% compare price per pack. A skills audit shows 16 of 42 operatives have not used the new flaking rollers; short courses at the college cost $680 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Golden Acre Cereals as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, raising the cost of GAC's $400,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $12.40 to $13.29 an hour from April 2026. (3) Wheat and oat input prices have risen 11.3% year-on-year, food-price inflation is 7.4% and spending on breakfast cereals grew 2.6%.

questions.question_text: GAC has financed its $460,000 expansion with a $400,000 bank loan and $60,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for GAC of using the bank loan rather than relying only on retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $400,000 bank loan gives GAC the full capital immediately, so the $460,000 flaking and packing line can be installed in one stage rather than waiting years to accumulate retained profit. For a cooperative with only $60,000 retained, waiting would delay the automation needed to cut the 6.1% packaging waste and the 2.9% defect rate, risking the trust of the regional grocers it supplies.

Point 2: Using the loan preserves GAC's limited retained profit for day-to-day working capital and for the $680 per employee short courses needed by 16 of 42 operatives. Repayments are spread over ten years, so the cost is matched to the years of benefit from the new line and does not consume the $12.00 selling price all at once. Interest is also tax-deductible in many systems, and the loan leaves member funds untouched, which suits a cooperative accountable to its members, unlike a share issue which a cooperative cannot use.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: GAC is launching a new high-fibre cereal. Consider television advertising, in-store demonstrations, or social media competitions. Which should GAC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television advertising: TV can build awareness of the high-fibre range across a wide region quickly, which could help GAC win listings beyond its current regional grocers. However, airtime and production are very costly for a cooperative carrying a $400,000 loan, and much of the audience will not shop in its distribution area, so spend is wasted. The 39% of surveyed shoppers who compare price per pack may also ignore a glossy advert.

In-store demonstrations: Demonstrations at the grocers that already stock GAC let shoppers taste the cereal and ask about fibre, directly using the 61% who prefer recyclable cartons and the 39% who compare price per pack. Staff can explain the new flaking process and show the carton. The limit is reach: only shoppers visiting those stores see it, and a workforce of 42 with 16 of 42 operatives still needing training may struggle to staff events.

Social media competitions: Competitions are cheap, measurable and can target health-conscious shoppers, and they can showcase the recyclable carton preferred by 61% of 450 respondents. They generate engagement quickly but may attract entrants who never buy cereal, and a cooperative with hierarchical, autocratic leadership may find it hard to respond fast to online feedback.

Recommendation: GAC should choose in-store demonstrations. They convert the 61% carton preference into actual trial at the point of sale, fit the regional grocer channel, and need no expensive media buy. Television is rejected as unaffordable and too broad for a $460,000 expansion with a $400,000 loan; social competitions are rejected because engagement does not equal sales and the 39% price-focused shoppers need a direct reason to switch.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses at least two options with advantages and disadvantages applied to GAC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of GAC with a justified recommendation and clear rejection of the alternatives.

questions.question_text: GAC's labour turnover is rising and packaging waste has reached 6.1%. Explain two benefits for GAC of using job rotation to improve motivation and reduce waste.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation moves the 42 operatives between flaking, packing and quality checks, breaking the repetitive work that has pushed complaints up from 19 to 31 a month. Greater variety reduces boredom and labour turnover, keeping experienced workers who know how to avoid the 6.1% packaging waste and the 2.9% defect rate, so GAC protects the 17,800 units milled last quarter.

Point 2: Rotation builds a more flexible workforce, so when 16 of 42 operatives still need training on the new flaking rollers, trained colleagues can cover different stations. This supports the $460,000 automated line and reduces reliance on the $680 per employee courses. Because GAC is hierarchical, rotation also gives workers a broader view of the process, helping them spot waste earlier and protecting the $12.00 selling price through more consistent quality. Satisfied, multi-skilled staff are also more likely to stay, cutting the disruption caused by rising labour turnover, and they can produce the recyclable cartons preferred by 61% of surveyed shoppers with fewer packing errors.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: GAC needs a new quality supervisor for the automated line. Consider promoting an existing operative or appointing someone from outside the business. Which should GAC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Promoting an existing operative: An internal promotion rewards a worker who already knows GAC's flaking rollers and quality standards, so supervision can start immediately with no induction period. It raises morale in a workforce of 42 where labour turnover is rising and complaints have grown from 19 to 31 a month, and it avoids recruitment fees. It is cheap compared with the $460,000 investment and complements the $680 short courses. The risk is that the promoted worker lacks supervisory experience and may keep old habits, which could leave the 6.1% packaging waste unchallenged under autocratic leadership.

Appointing from outside: An external candidate brings fresh quality-control methods and experience of automated lines, useful for cutting the 2.9% defect rate and for training the 16 of 42 operatives new to the rollers. It also injects new ideas into a hierarchical structure. The drawbacks are higher recruitment and induction costs, longer settling-in time, and possible resentment among existing staff who were passed over, which could worsen turnover.

Decision: GAC should promote an existing operative, supported by supervisory training. Internal promotion is faster, cheaper and directly tackles the motivation and turnover problem while preserving knowledge of the 17,800-unit process. It also keeps the $680 course budget available for the 16 of 42 operatives who still need roller skills. An external appointment is rejected because the extra cost and resentment risk are not justified while a $400,000 loan is being serviced and the existing team already needs retraining; outside expertise can be brought in later as a short consultant if the 2.9% defect rate does not improve.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment choices with limited application to GAC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both choices in the context of GAC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both choices in the context of GAC with a well-justified decision covering cost, knowledge and motivation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GAC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $210,000 / ($12.00 - $5.00) = $210,000 / $7.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.00 - $5.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GAC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 70,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 40,000 units, to decide whether to run the new flaking line at full capacity.
2. Use $7.00 contribution per unit to test pricing: if grocers demanded a $0.50 discount, contribution would fall to $6.50, and managers could calculate the extra volume needed to keep profit unchanged.
3. Combine fixed costs of $210,000 with $7.00 contribution to set the annual volume needed to service the $400,000 bank loan, checking the $460,000 expansion before further borrowing.
4. Unit cost of $8.00 ($210,000 / 70,000 + $5.00) can be tracked monthly to detect the 6.1% packaging waste and the 2.9% defect rate, protecting the $12.00 price.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 40,000-unit margin of safety; pricing with a $0.50 discount; loan-service volume targets; unit-cost benchmarking at $8.00.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GAC's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GAC's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.29 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.21 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.68 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.55 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $110,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $28,000 cash = $233,000; 2025 current assets = $130,000 + $88,000 + $20,000 = $238,000. Cover of the 2024 current liabilities of $180,000 was $233,000 / $180,000 = 1.29; cover of the 2025 liabilities of $196,000 was $238,000 / $196,000 = 1.21. Liquid assets excluding inventories were $233,000 - $110,000 = $123,000 in 2024, giving $123,000 / $180,000 = 0.68, and $238,000 - $130,000 = $108,000 in 2025, giving $108,000 / $196,000 = 0.55.

Evaluation: Liquidity has deteriorated. Cover fell from 1.29 to 1.21 because current liabilities rose from $180,000 to $196,000 faster than current assets, which grew only from $233,000 to $238,000. The liquid-asset measure fell more sharply, from 0.68 to 0.55, because cash dropped from $28,000 to $20,000 and receivables fell from $95,000 to $88,000 while inventories rose from $110,000 to $130,000. More of GAC's short-term cover now depends on selling cereal stock, which is risky given the 6.1% packaging waste and 2.9% defect rate. Servicing a $400,000 loan while funding a $460,000 line leaves little headroom if grocers pay late.

Conclusion: GAC's liquidity has not improved. Both measures fell and the decline in liquid assets is the stronger warning, since it is not explained by a one-off stock build. GAC should slow the inventory rise and protect cash before taking on more debt.

mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of the current-asset components and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GAC of introducing automation in its packing process.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Automation can pack the 70,000 units more consistently than manual labour, directly reducing the 6.1% packaging waste and the 2.9% defect rate that have raised complaints from 19 to 31 a month. It also reduces dependence on the 16 of 42 operatives still learning the flaking rollers and supports the $460,000 investment by raising output without adding to the workforce of 42, protecting the $12.00 selling price through steadier quality.

Disadvantage: Automated packing equipment needs a large capital outlay on top of the $400,000 loan, and maintenance or breakdowns could halt the line entirely, leaving GAC unable to supply regional grocers. It may also displace workers at a time when labour turnover is already a problem, hurting morale in a cooperative. The $680 per employee short courses would need to be expanded to teach operatives to run and maintain the machines, adding cost and time while wheat and oat prices rise 11.3%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in wheat and oat input prices will affect GAC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): The change is 0.75 percentage points. If GAC's $400,000 variable-rate loan is not fixed, the added annual interest is 0.75% x $400,000 = $3,000, modest beside fixed costs of $210,000 and a $460,000 expansion. A fixed-rate loan would mean no immediate extra cost. Higher rates may slow grocer orders and raise future borrowing costs, but this is a manageable, predictable item.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $13.29): GAC employs 42 workers, but the insert states no hours worked and no individual wages, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. Productivity is 70,000 units / 42 staff = about 1,667 units per worker. If productivity is maintained, the rise can be absorbed within the $5.00 variable cost and $7.00 contribution; if labour turnover and the 6.1% waste persist, unit labour costs rise. This is a permanent rise but cannot be quantified honestly from the insert.

Input price inflation (11.3% wheat and oats): The insert does not break down the $5.00 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is valid: if all of the $5.00 rose 11.3%, that is 11.3% x $5.00 = about $0.57 per unit, or around $39,000 a year at 70,000 units. That directly cuts the $7.00 contribution funding the $400,000 loan. GAC can partly recover it through the 61% preference for recyclable cartons, but the 39% who compare price per pack limit price increases.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in wheat and oat prices will have the greatest impact. It recurs on all 70,000 units and erodes the contribution that services the loan, far outweighing the $3,000 interest effect; the wage rise is also serious but unquantifiable and partly offset if productivity holds, while ingredient inflation hits the margin directly and repeatedly.
